sources.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
sources.text: Nvidia 's stock slid 4.12% Monday in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation , leading a broader chipmaker selloff after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week. The continued decline since Huang's resignation brought Nvidia's stock to its lowest close since July 1, 2025. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday. An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk , rallied behind him. A source familiar with the matter told CNBC, however, that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Huang. Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom. Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls. — CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

sources.title: Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO becomes a political proxy war
sources.text: Huang’s exit sharpens debate over US stance towards Beijing; and as outages increase, do you get the feeling nothing works? This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here . Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers. The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang ’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender. We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era. The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls. Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients. Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned . Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions. The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China , given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them. Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose. Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left. Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him. The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang. Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder. “This week is seeing a long overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán , a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “ key man risk ”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible. “Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said. Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are not likely successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis. Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue . ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. sources.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
sources.text: Huang resigned last week over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC . Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday , after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there. The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him. Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications . Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues. The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions. Huang’s full statement is published below. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me. I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

sources.text: In his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO last week, Jensen Huang struck a contrite tone, saying that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence contact. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in the written statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation." Huang said he had seen support from investors and employees and was willing to come back as CEO to help the company navigate "complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics." "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in the statement. Sources told CNBC Monday that the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO, putting together an online petition with more than 180,000 signatures. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang, Nvidia's founder, admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had a liason with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence. Jensen Huang also reportedly had romances with employees at Nvidia. Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. Its board of directors said on Friday that it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
sources.text: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips. Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch. Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes. But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. sources.title: NVIDIA establishes export control committee following Jensen Huang resignation
sources.text: The company’s existing global trade compliance team will report to the new committee. Following Jensen Huang's resignation last week , NVIDIA's board of directors has established a new oversight committee to oversee the company's ongoing compliance with US export controls. Suzanne Nora Johnson , a former Goldman Sachs vice chair and recent NVIDIA board appointee, will lead the new internal organization, dubbed the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. The company's existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new committee, as well as interim CEO Colette Kress , on its day-to-day operations. NVIDIA adds the committee will meet at least once quarterly, with meetings with the company's management included. NVIDIA did not immediately respond to a question from Engadget regarding whether the new committee would have the power to halt sales its compliance staff flags, or if it would merely be limited to escalating such issues to Kress and the company's board of directors. In its press release, NVIDIA did say the committee would include two other directors as members, Stephen Neal and John Dabiri . "We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," said Harvey Jones, chairman of NVIDIA's board. According to Alex Jacquez , senior vice president of policy, advocacy and research at the economic think tank Groundwork Collaborative , NVIDIA's decision to create this committee at this specific moment raises the question of why the company needs to implement new protocol if it was previously complying with US export laws. "How much is theater for the board and Trump administration to signal that they're taking this seriously, and how much is actual reevaluation of existing practices is still to be determined," he said. The timing of the announcement comes as NVIDIA and its former CEO face increased scrutiny over the company's compliance with US export controls to China. When reporting of Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset, first surfaced, NVIDIA's board said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised." In a joint statement issued Monday alongside the Department of Justice , the US Commerce Department said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024. Alice Huang took a controlling stake in the Singaporean cloud computing company in 2023 before leaving it in August 2025. For part of that time, the firm was one of NVIDIA's business partners in the Asia-Pacific region. The Commerce Department says it requested documents from NVIDIA involving "direct or indirect" sales to Megaspeed in May 2025. In June of that same year, the company placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list. According to The Information , Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have facilitated at least $7.5 billion in NVIDIA GPU sales to China. The former CEO has agreed to a closed-doors, transcribed interview with multiple House committees on December 1 . Update 12:15PM ET : Added commentary from Alex Jacquez, senior vice president of policy, advocacy and research at Groundwork Collective.

stories.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
stories.summary: Turn Gemini’s annotations into an edge model for manufacturing inspection. Explore three prompting approaches, review labels, and train RF-DETR model with Roboflow. Deploy the trained model near the camera and keep Gemini available to inspect difficult cases and improve future training data.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
sources.text: To distill Gemini into an edge model, have Gemini label your images, review and correct those labels, then train a small detector that runs next to the camera and does the routine inspections. In Roboflow, auto-label with Gemini through a class description, the Auto Label agent or an Open Prompt Workflow. Then train RF-DETR Small on the reviewed dataset, run it with Inference on your edge device, and route uncertain cases back to Gemini or a human reviewer. Checking an assembly for missing screws takes more than counting detections. A model might miss one screw and mistake a reflection for another, returning the expected count while overlooking an incomplete product. A useful inspection system needs to locate the visible screws at each mounting position and flag images that need further review. With Roboflow, you can use Gemini to help build the training dataset for that system, then train a compact RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) model to detect screws near the camera. In this approach to model distillation , Gemini generates candidate bounding boxes, you review and correct the annotations, and RF-DETR learns the specific detection task. At deployment, the smaller model handles routine detection, while routing logic sends selected difficult images to Gemini or a person for review. In this guide, you’ll explore three ways to prompt Gemini for screw annotations: class descriptions in Roboflow Auto Label, conversational feedback with the Auto Label agent, and an Open Prompt Workflow that returns boxes for inspection in Python. You’ll then review the labels, train RF-DETR Small, test it on your edge hardware, and configure a fallback for uncertain results. Before generating labels, decide exactly what one object means. In our reference image, each screw annotation covers the full visible fastener region, including its outer exposed end and inner metal feature. One screw receives one box. This definition must stay the same across the dataset. Create an Object Detection project and upload the product images (opens in a new tab) . Include complete products, missing screws, reflections, and realistic changes in lighting. In Roboflow Auto Label (opens in a new tab) , the class description is the prompt Gemini uses to find the object . Follow these steps. Gemini searches using that description, and Auto Label saves each resulting annotation as screw . The expected count of four is an application rule. It should not force the teacher to produce four boxes when a screw is missing. You can also describe the labeling task through Chat with Auto Label agent . The agent builds a labeling Workflow from the model and classes and shows a preview. Use the conversation to refine what it should label. sources.title: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how
sources.text: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats. Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history. ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.” Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027 (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction. stories.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
stories.summary: After a shocking downfall, Nvidia’s CEO is out of a job. WIRED’s Lauren Goode explains what that means for the world’s most critical chip company, the AI industry, and Jensen Huang himself.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
sources.text: I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind. These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy. WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event , and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind? LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025. It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has. Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way. There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”? It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into. Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable. I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise. What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate. You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board? I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue. I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China. This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature. Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED , that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out. I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again. Oh, you don’t want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time? No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback. But this firm, it’s a reall
